subject: How modelling sex affects density and pmix estimates

messages.author: 72f2ccabe1e5089f
messages.subject: How modelling sex affects density and pmix estimates
parts:
Hi
I know there are different ways to model sex in secr and I have been trying to find confirmation of how the different approaches affect estimates of density and pmix (most examples focus on sex-specific detection parameters). I have read some of the vignettes and trawled through the google group as I know this issue has probably been raised here before but have not found a thread that completely addresses all my queries. Apologies for the duplication but I hope it will also be useful to others to have the info in one place. Here are the specific queries / points to clarify for the different approaches:


Modelling sex as a group or by separating the data into sessions. These two approaches are essentially equivalent (though I know one should not mix the approaches). 

1. If one models D ~ 1 is it correct that the sexes are constrained to have equal density and one would need to double the estimate to get the total density? And equal densities then mean that a 1:1 sex ratio is implied? 

2. If one models density with D ~ session or D ~ g, is it correct that one would get the sex-ratio from the sex differences in density?


Modelling sex as an individual covariate with CL = T. 

3. I know density is derived with this approach and one can estimate group specific densities. The difference in detection functions would lead to different derived densities for each sex, would one again estimate the sex-ratio from the differences in density?


Modelling sex as a hybrid mixture model. 

4. I know that this approach also estimates the sex-ratio via pmix. Is it correct that if one models D ~ 1 then the reported density is the total density of both hybrid classes? 

5. What happens with the pmix estimate if one chooses to model D ~ h2? Does it then come from the difference in the two density estimates?


Many thanks


Greg

Apologies for the duplication but I hope it will also be useful to others to have the info in one place. Here are the specific queries / points to clarify for the different approaches:


Modelling sex as a group or by separating the data into sessions. These two approaches are essentially equivalent (though I know one should not mix the approaches). 

1. If one models D ~ 1 is it correct that the sexes are constrained to have equal density and one would need to double the estimate to get the total density? And equal densities then mean that a 1:1 sex ratio is implied?
2. If one models density with D ~ session or D ~ g, is it correct that one would get the sex-ratio from the sex differences in density?

Modelling sex as an individual covariate with CL = T. 

3. I know density is derived with this approach and one can estimate group specific densities. The difference in detection functions would lead to different derived densities for each sex, would one again estimate the sex-ratio from the differences in density?

Modelling sex as a hybrid mixture model. 

4. I know that this approach also estimates the sex-ratio via pmix. Is it correct that if one models D ~ 1 then the reported density is the total density of both hybrid classes?
5. What happens with the pmix estimate if one chooses to model D ~ h2? Does it then come from the difference in the two density estimates?

D~h2 doesn't work: finite mixtures are for detection parameters only.


Many thanks


Greg


# Sex-specific analyses

library(secr)
setNumThreads(12)
old <- options(warn = -1)  

# create a dataset with 'sex' as covariate
ch <- captdata
covariates(ch) <- data.frame(sex = factor(sample(c('F','M'), 76, replace=TRUE)))

# sex as group, constant group density
fitgp1 <- secr.fit(ch, model = list(D~1, g0~g), groups = 'sex', trace = FALSE)
predict(fitgp1)

# sex as group, group-specific density
fitgp <- secr.fit(ch, model = list(D~g, g0~g), groups = 'sex', trace = FALSE)
predict(fitgp)

# sex as session, session-specific density
chfm <- split(ch, covariates(ch)$sex)
fitfm <- secr.fit(chfm, list(D~session, g0~session), trace = FALSE)
predict(fitfm)
derived(fitfm)

# sex as individual covariate
fitCL <- secr.fit(ch, g0~sex, CL = TRUE, trace = FALSE)
derived(fitCL)
derived(fitCL, groups = 'sex')

# sex as finite mixture (hybrid mixture model)
fith2 <- secr.fit(ch, g0~h2, hcov = 'sex', trace = FALSE)
predict(fith2)
derived(fith2, groups = 'sex')


# combining hybrid mixture for detection and
fith2D <- secr.fit(ch, hcov = 'sex', list(D~h2,g0~h2))
# Error in D.designdata(mask, model$D, grouplevels, session(capthist), sessioncov) :

Thanks for this very relevant chat!  If you want to derive the total population density for the model without an effect of sex on density (fitgp1 <- secr.fit(ch, model = list(D~1, g0~g), groups = 'sex', trace = FALSE), how do you get the confidence intervals around the total density?  You can double the mean estimate but how should you treat the SE or confidence intervals?

Thankyou,
Bron

I have read some of the vignettes and trawled through the google group as I know this issue has probably been raised here before but have not found a thread that completely addresses all my queries. Apologies for the duplication but I hope it will also be useful to others to have the info in one place. Here are the specific queries / points to clarify for the different approaches:


Modelling sex as a group or by separating the data into sessions. These two approaches are essentially equivalent (though I know one should not mix the approaches). 

1. If one models D ~ 1 is it correct that the sexes are constrained to have equal density and one would need to double the estimate to get the total density? And equal densities then mean that a 1:1 sex ratio is implied? 

Yes to both.

2. If one models density with D ~ session or D ~ g, is it correct that one would get the sex-ratio from the sex differences in density?

Yes

Modelling sex as an individual covariate with CL = T. 

3. I know density is derived with this approach and one can estimate group specific densities. The difference in detection functions would lead to different derived densities for each sex, would one again estimate the sex-ratio from the differences in density?

Yes

Modelling sex as a hybrid mixture model. 

4. I know that this approach also estimates the sex-ratio via pmix. Is it correct that if one models D ~ 1 then the reported density is the total density of both hybrid classes? 

Yes

5. What happens with the pmix estimate if one chooses to model D ~ h2? Does it then come from the difference in the two density estimates?

D~h2 doesn't work: finite mixtures are for detection parameters only.


Many thanks


Greg


# Sex-specific analyses

library(secr)
setNumThreads(12)
old <- options(warn = -1)  

# create a dataset with 'sex' as covariate
ch <- captdata
covariates(ch) <- data.frame(sex = factor(sample(c('F','M'), 76, replace=TRUE)))

# sex as group, constant group density
fitgp1 <- secr.fit(ch, model = list(D~1, g0~g), groups = 'sex', trace = FALSE)
predict(fitgp1)

# sex as group, group-specific density
fitgp <- secr.fit(ch, model = list(D~g, g0~g), groups = 'sex', trace = FALSE)
predict(fitgp)

# sex as session, session-specific density
chfm <- split(ch, covariates(ch)$sex)
fitfm <- secr.fit(chfm, list(D~session, g0~session), trace = FALSE)
predict(fitfm)
derived(fitfm)

# sex as individual covariate
fitCL <- secr.fit(ch, g0~sex, CL = TRUE, trace = FALSE)
derived(fitCL)
derived(fitCL, groups = 'sex')

# sex as finite mixture (hybrid mixture model)
fith2 <- secr.fit(ch, g0~h2, hcov = 'sex', trace = FALSE)
predict(fith2)
derived(fith2, groups = 'sex')


# combining hybrid mixture for detection and
fith2D <- secr.fit(ch, hcov = 'sex', list(D~h2,g0~h2))
